title: CBSL defends raising key rates to over two-year highs on inflation concerns | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:17
-     - 21

Governor 

Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe

Senior Deputy Governor Dr. Chandranath Amarasekara

Economic Research Department Director 

Dr. Lasitha Pathberiya

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) yesterday defended raising its key policy rate by 25 basis points to 9%, the highest since July 2024. It said the move would anchor inflation expectations, with headline inflation projected to reach 9% by end-November and stay elevated in the near term.

The Monetary Policy Board took the decision at its sixth and final review for 2026 on Thursday. It raised the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR), the CBSL’s main tool for signalling its monetary policy stance, from 8.75%. The Standing Deposit Facility Rate (SDFR) and the Standing Lending Facility Rate (SLFR) set the floor and ceiling for overnight interbank borrowing and are linked to the OPR with predetermined margins of ±50 basis points. They rose to 8.50% and 9.50%, respectively.

The Board also raised the Statutory Reserve Requirement (SRR) by one percentage point to 3%, from the reserve maintenance period starting 9 December. The SRR increase will permanently take about Rs. 150 billion out of the money market. The move is the second tightening this year, after the Board raised the OPR by 100 basis points in May.

“The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has lasted longer than expected,” the CBSL said. High global energy prices and rising food prices have kept pushing up domestic inflation, which reached 8.3% year-on-year in October. Core inflation also rose as higher energy and food prices spilled over. The CBSL said global energy prices have eased somewhat recently, but the second-round effects of earlier increases are expected to keep pressure on prices in the near term.

Economic Research Department Director Dr. Lasitha Pathberiya said headline inflation had climbed from 2.2% in March, while core inflation, which excludes volatile items, rose to 5.6% in October. He said the composition of inflation was now the bigger worry. “What matters most in this particular review is food and non-alcoholic beverages. You can see the spillovers from energy to food as well as services,” he said.

The CBSL’s latest projections show inflation could stay higher for longer than previously forecast before returning to the 5% target in the second half of 2027. Inflation expectations one year ahead have risen recently, although medium-term expectations remain anchored around the target.

“In view of the elevated inflation outlook in the near term, the Board was of the view that a further tightening of the monetary policy stance would be required to minimise the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations,” the CBSL said.

Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe said inflation had overshot the CBSL’s own forecasts. When the Board tightened in May, it expected inflation to stay below 8% and return to target in the first half of 2027. “But now it appears to remain at a higher level for longer than what we expected. That could have an impact on anchoring inflation expectations,” he said.

Inflation has risen this far even with fiscal support from fuel subsidies this year, Dr. Weerasinghe said. Journalists noted that a Rs. 40.65 billion diesel subsidy runs until end-December and asked what the CBSL had assumed for fuel prices from January. He said the Bank could not confirm those figures. Its projections rest on broad assumptions under which inflation stays around 9% for the next several months.

The Governor acknowledged that higher rates can do little about price increases that come from imported energy costs. “In the short term, what we do currently may not have a significant impact on inflation, but it will have a small signalling effect and help anchor inflation expectations,” he said. The hike is therefore aimed less at current prices than at stopping households and businesses from building a higher inflation rate into their wage demands and pricing decisions.

“There could be different reasons for inflation, but whatever the cause, it will erode the purchasing power of people,” Dr. Weerasinghe said.

He suggested the tightening may not last long. The Board will be guided by data on whether inflation returns as expected or faster. “Once we clearly see inflation is on the downward path, then we can go into an easing cycle again,” he said.

The CBSL also moved to curb the liquidity that is fuelling credit. The SRR is the share of customer deposits that commercial banks must keep with the Central Bank, so money held under it cannot be lent out. 

Senior Deputy Governor Dr. Chandranath Amarasekara said the normal SRR was 4%, and it was cut to 2% in 2023 to support liquidity in the banking system. Until 8 December, Sri Lanka will have the lowest SRR it has ever had. “You can think of this as SRR normalisation,” he said.

Dr. Pathberiya said the surplus came mainly from the CBSL’s foreign exchange purchases. The CBSL bought around $ 1.7 billion from the market up to October and continued to buy substantially in November. “We see the outstanding liquidity around Rs. 450 billion, and also overnight liquidity at higher levels,” he said.

The CBSL said the build-up could slow the moderation in credit expansion it wants to see. Until now it has absorbed the surplus temporarily through overnight, short-term and long-term auctions. Dr. Amarasekara said the SRR hike was the next step in normalising liquidity since the crisis.

Dr. Weerasinghe said the CBSL used the instrument sparingly. “SRR is not a traditional, conventional instrument to use for monetary policy purposes. That’s why we have not been using it quite regularly,” he said. “This is a good opportunity for us to use this instrument to absorb liquidity on a permanent basis.”

At around Rs. 450 billion, the surplus would still be around Rs. 300 billion after the SRR drain. That leaves the CBSL enough room to keep credit flowing while limiting excess lending. “Even if we take Rs. 150 billion, we have flexibility to inject more liquidity to be able to maintain short-term interest rates,” Dr. Weerasinghe said.

Critics call the SRR a tax on banks and ask why the CBSL has not issued long-term securities of its own or sold dollars to the Treasury for rupees. Dr. Weerasinghe dismissed CBSL securities. “That would be a competing instrument in the market. We don’t see a reason to do that,” he said.

He said the CBSL holds a large stock of Government securities that will become marketable next year, and another official said they will become plain fixed-rate instruments from March. For now, he said, the SRR is the best instrument because so much structural liquidity has built up. Once those securities are marketable, the CBSL could sell them outright to absorb liquidity.

The CBSL said the external sector has held up despite global uncertainty. Its net foreign exchange purchases, made while the Government was servicing its debt, lifted gross official reserves to around $ 7.1 billion by end-October, including the swap facility from the People’s Bank of China. The rupee remained broadly stable. 

Dr. Weerasinghe said the CBSL is committed to selling dollars to the Government when it needs them. If the Government bought dollars in the market itself, he said, it would add a large buyer and create volatility, citing petroleum imports worth about $ 4 billion last year.

The CBSL said it would assess incoming data and emerging risks and stands ready to act to stabilise inflation around the target, while supporting the economy to reach its potential over the medium term.

title: CBSL sees economy near potential as policy focus stays on inflation | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:16
-     - 19

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) says the economy is still growing close to its potential. It made clear that inflation, not growth, drove its decision to tighten policy.

“We haven’t made a projection on next year’s growth yet. Internally in our models, there are some indications that our economy is still growing close to the potential growth,” Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe said.

He said the output gap was still negative, meaning the economy is producing below its capacity. That usually signals limited demand pressure. It is consistent with the CBSL’s view that energy and food costs, rather than an overheating economy, are behind the rise in prices.

Dr. Weerasinghe said the CBSL does not target a specific growth rate. “Growth is something that will come out based on a lot of other policies. Our responsibility is to make sure economic growth is around the potential, going forward,” he said. Policy decisions are based on the outlook for inflation and the economy’s growth potential, taking account of both domestic and external demand.

The Middle East conflict is affecting the external accounts. Central Bank Economic Research Department Director Dr. Lasitha Pathberiya said the monthly current account had slipped into small deficits in recent months. Imports have risen gradually, mainly because of the fuel bill and vehicle imports, while exports have been robust.

Gross official reserves still rose to around $ 7.1 billion by end-October, the CBSL said, helped by its net foreign exchange purchases even while the Government was servicing its debt. The Bank said it would keep supporting the economy to reach its potential over the medium term while bringing inflation back to target.

title: Private credit growth cools to 21.8% but still runs high: CBSL | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:16
-     - 22

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka’s (CBSL) May tightening is showing up in market interest rates. Private sector credit growth is slowing but remains high, which is part of the reason for this week’s second rate hike.

Economic Research Department Director Dr. Lasitha Pathberiya said that since the 100-basis-point hike in May, the interbank call money rate has risen by 108 basis points and the one-year Treasury Bill rate by 146 basis points. The weekly prime lending rate, which banks charge their best corporate customers, rose by 166 basis points. Private sector credit growth slowed but was still around 21.8% year-on-year, with large monthly expansions in some months such as September.

Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe said rates are meant to cool lending across the economy, not to target particular sectors. “I don’t think we are looking at the interest rate to curtail credit in one sector against others,” he said. He named personal loans, pawning and financial services as among the faster-growing areas.

Defending pawning, he said many people, including farmers, use gold-backed loans to finance cultivation and repay them after the harvest. “It’s the easiest way to have some credit for people who don’t have normal, easy access to credit. It’s a reasonable interest rate compared to the informal market rate,” he said.

He said rising gold prices had increased the value of the assets people borrow against, and so the size of the loans. That raised the risk that borrowers would not settle if prices fell. “It’s good that we imposed a loan-to-value ratio of 70%. That minimises the risk, not only for the customer but also for the bank,” Dr. Weerasinghe said. A loan-to-value ratio caps a loan as a share of the value of the asset pledged.

He said the CBSL does not decide how banks allocate credit. It sets interest rates and provides liquidity, and banks and borrowers make the lending decisions.

The CBSL will keep its deposit rate cap on non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs). The cap follows a formula linked to Treasury Bill and Bond rates and is adjusted quarterly. Asked whether weaker NBFIs would lose out to stronger players as liquidity tightens, the Governor said many companies already pay below the ceiling. “The cap is there to prevent even registered finance companies offering unnecessarily high rates to attract deposits. That’s a risk,” he said.

title: Sri Lanka reaches 2 m tourist arrivals earlier for third successive year | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:15
-     - 12

Sri Lanka’s tourism industry has crossed the two-million visitor mark for the third consecutive year, reaching the milestone on 20 November, as the Government steps up efforts to surpass last year’s arrivals record and secure greater economic returns from the sector.

Announcing the achievement in Parliament yesterday, Tourism Deputy Minister Prof. Ruwan Ranasinghe said reaching the threshold despite geopolitical tensions, disruptions to international flight routes, rising aviation fuel costs and global economic uncertainty reflected the resilience of the industry and continued international confidence in Sri Lanka.

The two-millionth visitor milestone was marked by the arrival of a Russian family comprising mother Nataliya, father Sergei and daughter Anna.

The latest milestone was achieved considerably earlier than in the previous two years. Sri Lanka crossed two million arrivals on 26 December in 2024, following a six-year gap since 2018, and reached the mark on 17 November in 2025.

Prof. Ranasinghe also highlighted an improvement in arrival momentum, with average daily tourist arrivals rising to 7,480 during 10–20 November this year, compared with 7,130 during the corresponding period in 2025, representing a 4.9% increase.

He attributed the continued growth to the entry of new international airlines, expanded direct air connectivity, access to new source markets and strengthened destination promotion, while acknowledging the setbacks caused by Cyclone Ditwah in November 2025.

However, the Government’s focus is increasingly shifting beyond visitor numbers towards maximising the economic contribution of tourism. Prof. Ranasinghe said steps were being taken to improve the methodology used to estimate tourism earnings in line with international standards, taking into account changing economic conditions, exchange rates and visitor spending patterns since 2018.

The Deputy Minister said the objective was to establish a more accurate assessment of tourism’s contribution to the economy and use the data to shape long-term policies and development targets.

The next immediate target is to exceed the total arrivals recorded in 2025 before the end of this year, supported by expanded air connectivity, international promotional campaigns, new market development and improvements to tourism services.

title: IMF tranche expected before year-end: CBSL | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:12
-     - 17

Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe yesterday said the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Executive Board was expected to meet shortly and that he expected the tranche under the Seventh Review of Sri Lanka’s Extended Fund Facility (EFF) to be released before the end of the year.

He made the remarks at the Central Bank’s post-Monetary Policy Review media briefing. 

The IMF reached a staff-level agreement with Sri Lanka on the Seventh Review of its $ 3 billion EFF on 4 October, but made Board approval of the next tranche of about $ 345 million contingent on the Government presenting a 2027 Budget in line with program parameters and on adequate progress with debt restructuring. A staff-level agreement is the IMF team’s sign-off on policies, which the Fund’s Executive Board must then approve before money is released. 

Once the tranche is disbursed, total IMF support under the arrangement, approved on 20 March, 2023, will reach about $ 2.7 billion. The current program is due to end in March 2027. 

The Fund will now assess whether the 2027 Budget meets those parameters. On Wednesday, Fitch Ratings said the Budget is broadly aligned with the parameters of the IMF program, which should support the Seventh Review. 

Beyond the fiscal numbers, the IMF has made growth-enhancing reforms central to the program’s final stretch. The Fund warned that ‘delivering strong and inclusive growth requires creating an enabling environment’ through reforms. It recommended liberalising trade, modernising business and labour rules, broadening access to finance, advancing digital public infrastructure and closing infrastructure gaps. It also urged a medium-term revenue strategy to make the tax system more efficient and fair, and stronger public investment management to speed up capital spending, including Cyclone Ditwah recovery. 

The IMF also pressed the Government to ‘allow domestic fuel prices to adjust in line with international fuel price movements’, keeping cost-recovery energy pricing while protecting vulnerable groups through targeted, time-bound support. 

The CBSL said separately that gross official reserves rose to around $ 7.1 billion by end-October, including the swap facility from the People’s Bank of China, helped by its net foreign exchange purchases despite the Government’s debt service payments.

title: CEB swings to Rs. 38.7 b loss in 2025 as tariff cuts bite | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:12
-     - 16

Energy Minister 

Anura Karunathilaka

The Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) slipped into a net loss of Rs. 38.7 billion in 2025, after net profits of Rs. 141.6 billion in 2024 and Rs. 57.6 billion in 2023, figures presented to Parliament showed.

The utility earned Rs. 422.2 billion in total revenue from electricity sales against total expenditure of Rs. 486.3 billion during the year.

Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka was responding on Thursday (19) to a question from Opposition Samagi Jana Balawegaya Parliamentarian Dayasiri Jayasekara. He said the CEB’s revenue fell sharply after electricity tariffs were cut, while other income also declined from 2024. The average cost of generating one kilowatt-hour of electricity stood at Rs. 18.22 in January 2025.

“Although the CEB sold more electricity in 2025 and reduced its finance costs, these gains weren’t enough to offset the lower tariffs, higher power purchase costs and increased payments to rooftop solar producers,” he said.



Tariffs were revised several times over the three years. In 2023, they were raised by 66.2% before being cut by 14.5% and a further 18%. They were cut by 22% and then 22.5% in 2024, and by 20.8% in 2025 before a 15% increase.

Karunathilaka said the cuts had pushed the CEB’s costs above the revenue forecast under the cost-reflective pricing method, under which tariffs are set to recover the cost of supply. “That’s the reason for the loss,” he said.

The General Treasury provided no funds to the CEB in 2024 or 2025. In 2023, it provided Rs. 126.3 billion as an additional investment to cover the CEB’s payments to the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation.

The quality of coal procured for power generation was also raised. Jayasekara said 25 coal shipments had been ordered but only 19 had arrived, and those did not meet the required standard. Another five shipments were subsequently brought in, and one of them also failed to meet the standard.

He said China’s achievements in digital technology, innovation, industrial development, infrastructure and modernisation held lessons for Sri Lanka as it pursued economic recovery, digital transformation and public sector modernisation.

However, he said the success of the programs should be measured by how well officials applied what they learnt to improve public services, strengthen institutions and contribute to national development, not by the number of officials trained.

He urged alumni to stay connected and share their knowledge and experience, describing them as ambassadors of knowledge and living bridges of friendship between the two countries.

title: Shanakiyan challenges legality of  fast-tracked mineral extraction licences | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:10
-     - 15

ITAK MP Shanakiyan Rasamanickam

Ilankai Tamil Arasu Katchi (ITAK) Parliamentary Group Leader and Batticaloa District MP Shanakiyan Rasamanickam yesterday questioned the legal basis of the Government’s fast-tracked mineral extraction licensing system. He warned that faster approvals without adequate assessments could cause irreversible damage to natural resources and threaten the long-term sustainability of the construction industry.

Rasamanickam recalled campaigning against environmental destruction with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake before the latter came to power. “In the past, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake fought alongside me against environmental destruction. He was my comrade in those struggles. But today, I am fighting alone. This is deeply painful to me,” he said. He said protecting the environment must remain a consistent responsibility, whoever is in Government.

He raised the questions in Parliament under Standing Order 27(2), addressed to the Minister of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development. He asked whether the Government was using administrative guidelines to bypass legal and environmental safeguards on the extraction of sand, rock, gravel, soil and brick clay.

Rasamanickam pointed out that mineral extraction is already governed by the Mines and Minerals Act, No. 33 of 1992, its Amendment Act, No. 66 of 2009, and the related regulations. However, following a Cabinet decision of 6 July, 2026, Industry Guideline No. 01/2026, issued on 31 August, set up District Monitoring Committees and directed that licence applications be referred to them from 1 September.

He questioned whether guidelines that Parliament had not enacted, and that were not issued as regulations under existing law, could lawfully change established licensing procedures. He asked whether the Attorney General’s opinion had been obtained on their validity. He also asked whether the committees’ recommendations were binding on the Geological Survey and Mines Bureau (GSMB) Director General.

He also questioned whether environmental conditions, Government fees, transport permit requirements and monitoring procedures had been relaxed under the new system. If they had, he asked the Government to identify the legal provisions that allowed it. He further asked whether the seven-day period for processing applications was long enough for comprehensive technical, environmental and resource assessments.

Rasamanickam alleged that licences issued under the National People’s Power (NPP) Government had caused severe environmental damage in Batticaloa District, and presented photographs of affected areas in Parliament.

“Natural resources such as soil cannot simply be regenerated. Protecting these resources is essential. Over the past three months, serious environmental destruction has taken place in several parts of Batticaloa as a result of sand extraction licences issued under the National People’s Power Government,” he said.

He said local authorities in Batticaloa had struggled to obtain approvals while private applicants appeared able to secure licences through the district-level process. He asked the Government to explain the difference and to apply the process transparently, lawfully and consistently.

Rasamanickam asked the Government to table the guidelines, their amendments, the Cabinet decision and the related Cabinet memorandum. He also asked for district-wise data on licences issued and renewed in 2024, 2025 and 2026. He wanted the data to include applications received since September, rejections, pending applications and average processing times. He also asked whether the Government had studied the impact of faster licensing on mineral reserves, extraction volumes and environmental sustainability, and whether it would present those studies to Parliament.

Arguing that mineral resources are finite, he asked whether the Government had a national policy promoting manufactured sand, alternative construction materials, recycling of construction waste and sustainable mineral resource management. If not, he asked when it would introduce one, and when the current licensing arrangements would be brought within a legally established regulatory framework.

Rasamanickam also raised the Sapi Nagar incident, saying justice had still not been delivered four years on. He criticised NPP representatives who had spoken out on the incident in the past for staying silent now that they are in government.

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Sri Lanka (CA Sri Lanka) hosted a comprehensive post-Budget seminar last week to provide members, business leaders, tax professionals and policymakers with an in-depth analysis of the key economic, fiscal and taxation proposals in National Budget 2027.

Held at CA Sri Lanka, the seminar attracted over 700 participants, both in person and virtually. It featured leading experts from the public and private sectors, who shared insights on the Budget’s potential impact on economic growth, investment, taxation, exports, public finances and tax administration.

Speaking at the event, CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe said Budget 2027 marks a significant phase in Sri Lanka’s economic journey as the country moves from a period of stabilisation towards sustainable growth and development. He also spoke on the performance of the country’s revenue-generating agencies and highlighted the importance of maintaining fiscal discipline while strengthening foreign exchange earnings, investment and economic resilience. He further stressed the importance of effective implementation in achieving the Budget’s growth objectives.

CA Sri Lanka Faculty of Taxation Chairman Saman Srilal observed that the Budget places considerable emphasis on productive sectors of the economy through investments in export-oriented manufacturing, tourism, agriculture, technology, digitalisation and SMEs. He welcomed several tax measures, including personal income tax relief, investment incentives to encourage export-oriented projects, and initiatives to strengthen tax administration and improve compliance processes.

Delivering the Budget highlights, EY Sri Lanka Partner and Head of Tax Sulaiman Nishtar gave a detailed overview of the Budget proposals and the legislative process. He highlighted the Government’s strategic focus on investment promotion, export development, digital transformation, infrastructure development, energy security and public sector modernisation. He also outlined several tax and regulatory measures designed to enhance Sri Lanka’s competitiveness and improve the overall business environment.

Offering an independent economic perspective, Verité Research Executive Director and Head of Research Dr. Nishan de Mel discussed the broader fiscal and economic implications of the Budget. He acknowledged the emphasis on the digital economy, renewable energy and export growth, while drawing attention to areas requiring continued policy focus, including labour force participation, higher education and public sector reform.

Representing the Government’s policy perspective, Finance Ministry Tax Policy Advisor Tanuja Perera provided insights into several tax proposals announced in the Budget, including revisions to personal income taxation, withholding tax measures and reforms relating to digital and cross-border taxation. She explained the policy rationale behind these proposals and how they are intended to help maintain fiscal sustainability while providing targeted relief to taxpayers.

Addressing developments in tax administration, Inland Revenue Department Commissioner P. Nandan Kumara outlined ongoing efforts to modernise the tax system through digitalisation, improved taxpayer services and greater inter-agency integration. He highlighted plans to advance the Department’s transition towards a more efficient, technology-driven tax administration framework.

The panel discussion also featured John Keells Holdings PLC Vice President and Head of Corporate Finance, Group Tax and Social Entrepreneurship Nisreen Rehmanjee, who shared practical perspectives from the corporate sector on tax compliance, taxpayer facilitation and broadening the tax base. The discussion was moderated by BDO Partners Partner and Head of Tax Sarah Afker.

People’s Bank and the Justice and National Integration Ministry have signed an agreement to implement an Internet Payment Gateway (IPG) for accepting court-related payments electronically, marking another significant milestone in Sri Lanka’s judicial digital transformation journey.

Justice and National Integration Ministry Secretary Ayesha Jinasena PC and People’s Bank Chairman Chandana Guniyangoda exchanged the agreement recently at the Justice Ministry premises in Colombo 10. People’s Bank Payments and Cards Deputy General Manager I.K. Indika, along with Card Centre officials and representatives of the Justice Ministry, also participated in the event.

The partnership further strengthens the longstanding collaboration between the two institutions in introducing convenient, secure and efficient digital payment facilities across the country’s judicial system.

The Internet Payment Gateway will further expand these facilities by enabling court users to make applicable payments through online channels, reducing the need for physical visits to court payment counters or bank branches. This is expected to provide greater convenience to litigants, Attorneys-at-Law and other members of the public accessing judicial services.

The initiative is aligned with the Government’s broader digital transformation agenda and the E-Courts Project, which aims to modernise Sri Lanka’s judicial administration through technology-driven solutions, improve operational efficiency, enhance transparency and facilitate better access to justice.

“The digital transformation of the judicial system is an important priority in our efforts to improve the efficiency, accessibility and transparency of the administration of justice. The introduction of an Internet Payment Gateway for court-related payments is a significant step towards creating a more convenient and technology-enabled judicial environment. This initiative will reduce the administrative burden associated with traditional payment methods and provide greater convenience to the public, including litigants and legal practitioners. We appreciate the continued cooperation and support of People’s Bank in facilitating the digital transformation of the judicial sector,” Jinasena said.

“People’s Bank is proud to be a strategic banking partner in supporting the digital transformation of Sri Lanka’s judicial system. title: Give citizens and regions chance, and Sri Lanka grows richer | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:10
-     - 14

The 13th Amendment gave the regions a voice in 1987; the 12 June framework would give promises a penalty. Together they turn development from a gift into an opportunity, and opportunity into shared prosperity and trust. The question is whether Parliament will act before the street, and a generation, makes the argument for it

Human development is driven by people, not delivered to them. The State must do its part. The 13th Amendment already gives every province the means. A country that lets its citizens and regions build will be richer for it

This autumn, from Paris to Tirana and Belgrade, Europe’s young are marching against rising costs and failing services. Young protesters give the same explanation: nobody heard us.

Sri Lanka knows that sentence. The grievance is the same: sacrifice without a fair share, a real say, or anyone answerable when promises fail. More than 300,000 Sri Lankans left for foreign employment in 2024. A State that loses its young loses its future.

And the first rung of the ladder is breaking. Stanford researchers find that since late 2022, employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the occupations most exposed to AI has fallen steadily behind their peers, a gap that has now widened to 19%, mainly because firms are simply not hiring them. The World Bank ranks Sri Lanka among South Asia’s most AI-exposed economies and last in jobs where AI complements workers rather than replaces them; nearly a quarter of our workforce is in exposed occupations. The clerical, call-centre and junior coding jobs our graduates queue for are the first to go. If Colombo cannot promise those first jobs, the regions must be free to create new ones, in work that needs local hands and local knowledge.

Recovery in the ledger, not yet in the kitchen

On paper, Sri Lanka has recovered: a primary surplus, rebuilt reserves, restructured debt. Households see otherwise. Poverty is near 17% nationally and 36% on the estates. In 2024 the Western Province produced 42.4% of national output; the North, 4.4%. For most of the country, development has been something done to it, not by it.

After 1987–89, the Presidential Commission on Youth heard young people say they could bear hardship but not deprivation with injustice. Its recommendations were shelved. Every uprising we have had followed one pattern: a voice unheard, a conflict escalated. The street is where unheard arguments go.

Do we give people the opportunity?

The 1986 UN Declaration on the Right to Development calls the human person the central subject of development: its active participant, not merely its beneficiary. That is the test Sri Lanka has failed since independence. In more than seventy-five years, no government has asked the regions what their development priorities are. Colombo has always decided. Decentralised budgets went to MPs, not regions; the District Development Councils of 1981 were stillborn; Provincial Councils have been starved of money and power since 1988. The outcome to date is four uprisings: the JVP insurrections of 1971 and 1987–89, a war in the North and East that consumed a generation, and the Aragalaya of 2022. We ask citizens to bear the cost, yet never let them, or their regions, decide what comes next.

Development is driven by the farmer, the fishing cooperative, the young coder in Vavuniya or Matara. The State’s role is large but supporting: guarantee the floor, share revenue fairly, build what no village can build alone.

The machinery we already have

The 13th Amendment of 1987 gave nine Provincial Councils 37 subjects of their own, among them agriculture, irrigation, health, education and provincial planning, and a Finance Commission to balance development across regions. Its intent was a measure of self-direction. That intent has been honoured mostly in the breach. Councils have gone nearly nine years without elections, most provincial money pays salaries, and subjects have drifted back to ministries.

The Praja Shakthi program shows the bottom-up instinct is alive: community councils in some 14,000 villages now propose local projects. But village councils that answer to a ministry, with no elected provincial tier above them, are a ladder missing its middle rungs. The 13th Amendment supplies those rungs. Using it needs no new constitution, only elections and the will to let elected councils decide.

Nine provinces, nine futures

Ask each province: what do your people want this place to be in ten years? Let the answer be a Provincial Development Charter, built from village assemblies upward, adopted by an elected council, costed, and tested against the minimums every citizen is owed. The State guarantees the floor and a formula-based share of revenue; the province chooses the path.

In the North, a charter might make the province the country’s most water-efficient farming region, owned through a farmer-majority Growers Federation and exporting across 64 kilometres to Tamil Nadu and to diaspora markets abroad. In the hill country, it would begin with dignity: land titles, housing and a route from estate labour to ownership. In the East, shared mills and fish markets could make coexistence pay. Some will fail. A province that tries and misses learns faster than a nation that waits for permission.

Others show it can work. In 1996 Kerala handed 35 to 40% of its development budget to local bodies; today its Kudumbashree women’s groups supply nearly a third of its local councillors.

Plan for the climate we have

Our plans are also written for a climate we no longer have. After floods and Cyclone Ditwah, the Meteorology Department now forecasts drought from January to April 2027 as a strong El Niño plays out. Yet budgets still treat floods, droughts, saline intrusion and coastal erosion as emergencies to answer afterwards, not conditions to design for.

Nor have we set out to harvest our waters. Monsoon rain runs off to the sea while the dry zone thirsts, and ancient tank cascades lie silted. At sea, an exclusive economic zone of 517,000 square kilometres, nearly eight times our land, yields little beyond overfished coastal waters, and about half the tuna caught on multi-day boats spoils before it reaches shore. Every provincial charter should begin with water: capturing and recharging fresh water, farming lagoons and reservoirs, and building cold chains so the sea’s catch becomes income, not waste. Regions know their hazards best. Let them plan for them.

Make the promise bind

Opportunity needs guarantees. The Sri Lanka Resilience and Accountability Framework, published in the Daily FT on 12 June, would turn development promises into obligations. It sets measurable targets in law, such as social protection of at least eight% of the budget and ten doctors per 10,000 people in every district. And it creates an independent commission able to sanction those who miss targets. A promise without a penalty is only a press release. Lenders, who audit our books while no one audits their impact, should meet the same standard. A public district dashboard would let every province see whether it is being heard.

Fairness must also reach within regions, to estate families, female-headed households, oppressed castes, persons with disabilities and informal workers. Equality cannot simply be devolved; it must be guaranteed.

Creators, contributors, custodians

Opportunity is a two-way bargain. Citizens create the jobs and revenue that fund every right, pay their taxes honestly, refuse bribes, and keep watch through the forums that write their province’s charter. The State’s side is to tax fairly, show results, and clear away the gatekeeping that strangles initiative.

The dividend

Will we not all be richer for it? The Western Province holds 28% of the people and produces 42% of output. The other eight provinces hold nearly three-quarters of the people, most of the land and water, and produce less than three-fifths. If they closed even half the gap in output per person with the West, the national economy would be roughly a quarter larger, without a rupee of new debt. That wealth will come not from Colombo but from people given the chance to build where they live.

The 13th Amendment gave the regions a voice in 1987; the 12 June framework would give promises a penalty. Together they turn development from a gift into an opportunity, and opportunity into shared prosperity and trust. The question is whether Parliament will act before the street, and a generation, makes the argument for it.

title: 2027 Budget: Opportunities, challenges, and way forward | Daily FT
summary:

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The effectiveness of the proposed budget will depend not just on the allocation of financial resources but also on the quality of implementation, institutional coordination, transparency and accountability. . Its ultimate success will depend on whether it can translate fiscal discipline into productive investment, economic recovery into sustainable growth and national economic progress into tangible improvements in the living standards of the people

The 2027 Budget presented to the Parliament of Sri Lanka represents more than an annual exercise in estimating Government revenue and expenditure. It reflects the Government’s broader economic vision and its policy direction towards transforming the national economy from a phase of economic stabilisation to a more sustainable, productive and growth-oriented development model. The important emphasis of the Budget is on strengthening domestic production, promoting investment, expanding export capacity, improving economic competitiveness and ensuring inclusive social development.

The 2027 Budget Speech sets out the Government’s medium-term economic objectives, fiscal management strategies, investment priorities and development proposals across key sectors of the economy. These proposals need to be examined within the context of Sri Lanka’s recent economic challenges, including the accumulated public debt burden, fiscal constraints, foreign exchange pressures, cost of living difficulties and the need to rebuild investor confidence. While economic stabilisation has created a foundation for recovery, achieving sustained economic growth requires structural reforms, greater productive capacity, improved institutional efficiency and a more competitive business environment. One of the most significant challenges facing the Government is striking an appropriate balance between maintaining macroeconomic stability and improving the living standards of the population. Fiscal discipline, increased Government revenue and prudent public debt management are essential to maintaining economic confidence and ensuring long-term financial sustainability. However, these objectives must be pursued alongside measures to address the cost of living, strengthen social protection, generate employment opportunities and improve access to essential public services. Economic growth alone cannot be considered successful unless its benefits are reflected in improved household incomes, better employment prospects and a higher quality of life for ordinary citizens.

Furthermore, the effectiveness of the proposed Budget will depend not just on the allocation of financial resources but also on the quality of implementation, institutional coordination, transparency and accountability. Improving the efficiency of State-owned enterprises, reducing unnecessary public expenditure, strengthening public sector governance and ensuring that development projects deliver measurable economic returns are equally important. In this regard, the Government must move beyond policy announcements and establish clear implementation mechanisms, measurable performance indicators and appropriate monitoring systems to ensure that Budgetary commitments translate into tangible economic outcomes.

Therefore, the 2027 Budget should be evaluated not simply as an annual financial statement, but as a strategic economic policy framework that will influence Sri Lanka’s future development path. Its ultimate success will depend on whether it can translate fiscal discipline into productive investment, economic recovery into sustainable growth and national economic progress into tangible improvements in the living standards of the people. The critical question is whether the policies and financial allocations proposed in the Budget are sufficiently practical, financially sustainable and effectively implementable to achieve the country’s long term economic transformation.

Macroeconomic outlook

The medium term economic outlook within the 2027 Budget aims to achieve sustainable economic growth of 7% or more per annum. To this end, the targets include maintaining a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP, reducing the Budget deficit to below 5%, increasing Government revenue to 16% in the medium term and 20% in the long term, and sustaining public investment at a level exceeding 4% of GDP. However, the fact that Government revenue for 2027 is estimated at 15.8% of GDP, combined with a substantial interest payment burden of Rs. 2,643 billion, highlights the challenges in achieving these targets.

Therefore, in addition to maintaining fiscal discipline, priority must be given to expanding domestic production capacity, diversifying exports, attracting foreign investment, fostering technological innovation and developing human resources. Ultimately, the success of the Budget is determined not only by achieving the stated financial targets, but by translating them into tangible economic outcomes, such as job creation, growth in public income and an improved standard of living.

Government revenue and expenditure

According to the summary of the 2027 Budget Estimates, total Government revenue and grants are projected at Rs. 6,180 billion, while total expenditure is estimated at Rs. 7,673 billion. These figures indicate that a significant gap persists between Government revenue and expenditure, resulting in an estimated Budget deficit of Rs. 1,493 billion. Notably, interest payments amounting to Rs. 2,643 billion account for approximately 34.4% of total Government expenditure and represent a substantial burden on public finances. This limits the fiscal space available for infrastructure development, social welfare programs and other essential public investments. Furthermore, the high level of interest payments highlights the continuing impact of accumulated public debt and the importance of maintaining long-term debt sustainability. Therefore, efforts to increase Government revenue should focus not only on raising taxes, but also on expanding economic activity, broadening the tax base, digitising tax administration, minimising tax evasion and enhancing the productivity of State-owned enterprises.

From a broader economic perspective, the key challenge facing the Government is not simply the reduction of the Budget deficit but the improvement of the quality and efficiency of public finances. Although increasing tax revenue is essential for fiscal consolidation, excessive reliance on indirect taxation could increase the cost of living, place additional pressure on businesses and discourage consumption and investment. At the same time, expenditure rationalisation should not come at the expense of essential development investments that generate future economic returns. The Government must therefore gradually shift its expenditure priorities from consumption-oriented spending towards productive capital investment, particularly in transport infrastructure, ports, logistics, energy, technology and export-oriented industries. In addition, improving the financial performance of State-owned enterprises, strengthening public procurement and introducing measurable performance targets for public expenditure are essential. Ultimately, the success of the 2027 Budget should be assessed not merely by its ability to achieve short-term fiscal targets, but by whether it can create a sustainable revenue base, reduce the debt burden and generate sufficient economic growth to improve the country’s long-term fiscal position.

Public investment and development projects

A notable feature of the 2027 Budget is the focus on increasing public investment. According to the summary of Budget estimates, public investment for the year 2027 is set at Rs. 1,750 billion; meanwhile, the Budget speech mentions a broader public investment target of Rs. 2,000 billion, which includes supplementary provisions. These investments encompass a range of sectors, including education, health, transportation, roads, agriculture, housing, energy, and digital infrastructure. However, the success of public investment is not determined solely by the amount of funds allocated. It is also essential to ensure the timely completion of projects, transparency in the procurement process, cost control, and the assessment of returns on investment. In particular, priority must be given to completing projects that were initiated in the past but subsequently stalled, ensuring the effective utilisation of existing infrastructure, and conducting rigorous feasibility studies for new projects.

Development of transport and road infrastructure

The 2027 Budget proposes an allocation of Rs. 95 billion for the modernisation of transport and road infrastructure. Key proposals under this initiative include expanding the metro bus service to major cities, providing the necessary facilities for 100 electric buses, procuring 200 small buses to strengthen rural transport, acquiring five railway carriages, and modernising railway stations. Furthermore, investments have been proposed for the expansion of the highway network, including the Central and Ruwanpura Expressway projects.

These investments are expected to reduce transit times and operational costs, improve market access, and expand regional economic activity. However, their success depends on the efficient implementation of projects, the control of costs and timelines, long-term maintenance, and a proper assessment of the economic and social returns generated by the use of public funds. Therefore, implementing these proposals with transparency and systematic management will contribute to enhancing national productivity and fostering sustainable economic growth.

Education, human resources and skills development

The 2027 Budget proposes the allocation of funds for the education and vocational training sectors, with the objective of creating a workforce equipped with the knowledge and technical skills required to meet future economic demands. Accordingly, it is proposed to allocate Rs. 4,000 million for the digitalisation of general education, Rs. 2,000 million for human resource development within the education sector, Rs. 1,500 million for the modernisation of technical and vocational colleges, and Rs. 800 million for the development of facilities at the University of Vocational Technology.

The primary objective of these investments is to develop human resources capable of adapting to technological changes and possessing skills that align with the demands of the job market. However, the success of these programs should not be evaluated solely based on the amount of funds allocated or the scale of physical facilities provided; rather, it should be assessed through measurable indicators such as the development of students’ skills, post-vocational training employment rates, alignment with the labor market, and outcomes in research and innovation. Consequently, it is essential that investments in education are implemented in a manner that strengthens the nation’s human capital and contributes to long-term economic growth.

Digital economy and innovation

Integrating digital technology into every sector of the economy is a key policy direction in the 2027 Budget. Proposals such as the establishment of a Digital Economy Authority and a National Digital Economy Council, the strengthening of cybersecurity, and the digitalisation of public services aim to create a new digital ecosystem. Another significant aspect is the allocation of Rs. 23,800 million for research and development programs. To derive tangible economic benefits from these investments, collaboration must be strengthened among research institutions, universities, private companies, and public sector entities. It is particularly important to develop local capabilities in areas such as artificial intelligence, data analytics, automation, software development, and technology-driven entrepreneurship.

Agriculture and the rural economy

The 2027 Budget focuses on enhancing agricultural productivity and strengthening the rural economy. Although approximately 23.9% of the national workforce is engaged in agriculture, its contribution to the national economy stands at only about 8.4% a figure that underscores the need to improve productivity and the adoption of technology within this sector. Accordingly, key proposed measures include promoting collective farming methods, expanding the use of agricultural machinery, improving product quality and market access, modernising agrarian service centers, and incentivising private sector investment. The success of these initiatives will be determined by their ability to increase farmer incomes, minimise post-harvest losses, and enhance the competitiveness of domestic agricultural products.

SMEs and export growth

Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) make a vital contribution to Sri Lanka’s economy. It is essential to provide these enterprises with financial facilities, technical support, market access, and business training. The 2027 Budget proposes modernising the existing TIEP (Temporary Importation for Export Processing) scheme to help small and medium-scale industrialists enter export markets. Furthermore, proposals have been put forward to expand the existing Free Trade Agreement with India, explore a new agreement with China, and engage in regional trade frameworks such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP). However, the success of these policies does not depend solely on the signing of agreements. It is also necessary to ensure that local producers are able to manufacture goods at competitive prices, meet quality standards and maintain consistent access to international markets.

Health and social protection

Ensuring the equitable distribution of the benefits of economic development among the people is another key objective of the 2027 Budget. Provisions have been proposed to enhance healthcare facilities, procure medical equipment, expand ambulance services, and strengthen regional health infrastructure. Furthermore, the Budget incorporates social protection programs for low-income families, persons with disabilities, the elderly, and those affected by disasters. The focus here extends beyond the mere provision of subsidies; it aims to improve the income generating capacity of these groups and enhance their opportunities to participate in the economy.

Key challenges and risks for the Budget

The successful implementation of the development proposals in the 2027 Budget faces several key challenges, including the burden of public debt and high interest payments, delays in project execution alongside rising costs, the risks posed by inflation and the increasing cost of living and concerns regarding the efficiency of State institutions. Furthermore, external factors such as geopolitical crises in the Middle East, fluctuations in international energy prices, climate change and natural disasters could also impact Sri Lanka’s economic stability. In particular, given the burden of total interest payments amounting to Rs. 4,850 billion, the efficient management of public financial resources is essential for future stability of economy. Consequently, it is crucial to prioritise transparency, accountability, the monitoring of project progress and timely policy adjustments during the implementation of the Budget proposals.

The way forward

To swiftly translate the objectives of the 2027 Budget into tangible, practical outcomes, it is essential to establish a mechanism for monthly and quarterly progress reviews regarding the utilisation of Budgetary allocations and to expedite delayed development projects. Furthermore, it is important to introduce Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for State institutions and implement a results based evaluation framework. The accelerate the digitalisation of tax administration and public services another important factor. The expand financial and technical support for small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs). Additionally, economic stability can be strengthened by enhancing supply chain efficiency and market competitiveness, rather than relying solely on price controls.

Long term measures

To ensure that long term economic growth, priority must be given to building an export oriented production economy, promoting research and innovation and developing human resources with skills suited to the international job market. Furthermore, it is essential to expand the use of renewable energy, strengthen public-private partnerships with transparency and enhance the financial and operational efficiency of State-owned enterprises. Additionally building an economic and social system resilient to climate change and natural disasters can secure the country’s long-term economic stability and sustainable development.

The 2027 Budget aims to advance the process of stabilising Sri Lanka’s economy by fostering an economic transformation rooted in production, investment, exports, technology and social equity. Its success hinges on establishing a coherent alignment between the proposals presented in the Budget speech and the financial allocations set out in the Appropriation Bill. Furthermore, it is essential that the allocated funds are utilised in a timely manner, in accordance with the correct priorities, and in a way that yields measurable outcomes. The primary challenge facing Sri Lanka today lies not merely in maintaining economic stability, but in translating that stability into tangible development one that enhances the public’s income, employment opportunities, business growth and overall quality of life.

This requires robust public financial management an efficient public service, a responsible private sector, technological innovation and human resources equipped with knowledge. Ultimately, the true success of the 2027 Budget should be measured not by the amount of funds allocated or the number of development proposals announced, but by the value added to the national economy and the positive changes brought to the lives of the general public. The 2027 Budget represents another significant opportunity for Sri Lanka to transition from economic stability toward sustainable, productive and equitable development. Realising this opportunity is a collective responsibility shared by the Government, the private sector and the entire population.

Plastics and plastic waste pose major health risks because they break down into tiny particles (microplastics and nano plastics) and release thousands of toxic chemicals that enter the human body through air, food, water, and skin contact (https://www.genevaenvironmentnetwork.org/resources/updates/plastics-and-health/

While the attention on reducing or eliminating plastic waste is commendable, although the outcome of efforts is questionable, there does not seem to be a focus on reducing the use of plastic in day-to-day life. Many utility items are made from plastic, plastic in different forms are used in agriculture, in fisheries and in advertising materials (banners etc.). Most of these are not recycled or are recyclable, and after some time, they are disposed of by burying them or burning them. Environment risks are enormous, but health risks are even more damaging, but less known to the public to human beings and other living beings.

Although these guidelines highlight severe risks of lung cancer, stroke, low birth weight, and respiratory illnesses for women and children exposed to indoor plastic smoke, it is uncertain whether enough has been done to educate and increase public awareness of these dangers.

Environment risks are longer term risks and not tangible risks other than being eyesores to some. Few seem to understand the damage plastic waste does to the environment either due to lack of knowledge about it or due to the very common general apathy and indifference towards it.

Health risks on the other hand are short-, medium- and long-term risks, and they are tangible. title: The Vrindavan: The land of love | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 21 November 2026 00:00

By Nayak Adarsh Saubhagya

Some journeys are made to explore new places. Some are made to experience something beautiful. And then there are journeys that quietly change the way we look at life.

My journey to Vrindavan was one such experience.

I had always been fascinated by this sacred land of Shree Radha and Lord Krishna, the land of divine love. The devotion of its people, the stories of divine love, the temples, the saints, the sacred River Maa Yamuna, and the lives of those who surrender themselves to the path of Bhakti had always drawn my attention.

I went there with curiosity, devotion, and a desire to experience something beyond ordinary travel.

When I finally arrived in Vrindavan, I felt as though I had entered a different world. The narrow streets were filled with people, vehicles, pilgrims, monks, and wandering animals. Yet, amidst all the noise and movement, one expression seemed to connect everyone: “Radhe Radhe!”

People greeted one another with Radhe Radhe. Shopkeepers, strangers, pilgrims, and devotees seemed to carry the name wherever they went. It was more than a greeting; it felt like the heartbeat of the city, a city that seemed to breathe Radhe Radhe.

That evening, I visited Nidhivan, Seva Kunj, and Shri Banke Bihari Ji Temple. Each place had its own atmosphere and carried its own stories of devotion.

But something about my visit to Banke Bihari Ji was especially beautiful. I felt a quiet anticipation, almost as though I were going to meet someone very dear to me. And when I finally stood before Bihari Ji, I felt as if He had been waiting for me all along.

What a beautiful feeling! It was something beyond ordinary words.

But the most wonderful experience of my journey was yet to come.

The Braj Raj: The adorable and tender touch of the sacred soil of Vrindavan

That night, I came across a group of monks preparing to perform Parikrama, a circumambulation of the sacred land. I was fortunate to be the part of it, and we began walking barefoot. Before starting, we bowed down, touched the sacred dust of Vrindavan, known as Braj Raj, and applied it to our foreheads. I had heard people speak about the holiness of this soil. But that night, I experienced something that words can hardly capture. As we walked along the banks of the Yamuna, I began noticing something extraordinary about the soil.

It was incredibly soft.

The tiny particles felt delicate, almost like flower petals. The texture reminded me of freshly prepared laddus, made with flour and ghee—soft, delicate, and gentle to the touch. Every particle seemed to carry that tenderness. With every step, I felt as though the earth itself was receiving my feet. The soil seemed to make space for each step, welcoming me and allowing me to move forward. I did not feel that I was simply walking on the ground. It felt as though the land itself was lovingly accepting my presence, almost embracing my feet. For a moment, I felt connected to something much deeper than the physical surroundings. The sacredness of Braj Raj was no longer just a belief I had heard from others. It had become a personal experience of tenderness, humility, and surrender.

I cannot fully explain that feeling. Perhaps the sacredness of a place is not always understood through explanations. Sometimes, it is experienced through the simplest contact with nature.

That night, I was physically tired and eventually fell asleep, but the experience remained with me.

Beyond the robes: The heart of a seeker

The following day, I visited an ashram. I do not wish to mention its name. What matters here is not the identity of the place or the people, but what the experience made me reflect upon.

When I entered, I saw a monk sitting peacefully on a raised platform built around a tree. His eyes were closed, and he held a Japamala (prayer beads) in his hands. His face appeared completely immersed in bliss. I stood there for a moment, observing the stillness around him. Suddenly, he opened his eyes and noticed my footwear. In a loud voice, he instructed me to remove my slippers, as wearing footwear inside the ashram, especially on the sacred soil of Vrindavan, was not permitted.

I immediately removed them. I respected the tradition and continued walking. However, something about the interaction stayed with me. The monk who had appeared so peaceful in meditation had spoken with such harshness. I could not understand the contrast.

Later, I was directed towards a place where Prasad was being distributed. It was around noon, and what I witnessed there was remarkable. Thousands of sadhus and other people were seated, waiting for food. Volunteers were serving meals to everyone. There was an abundance of food, and people were waiting patiently to receive it.

I stood there, observing the entire scene.

While looking around, I noticed a person holding a Japamala inside a cloth covering commonly used while performing Japa. His index finger remained outside the covering. I remembered hearing that, according to certain traditions, the index finger should not touch the beads during Japa because it is associated with the ego.

This made me think about the symbolism behind the practice. If the entire body belongs to God, why is one finger considered unsuitable for touching something sacred?

At that very moment, I noticed the same person pointing his index finger towards another individual and shouting angrily:

“Hey! Don't you know that using a mobile phone is prohibited here?”

I smiled.

The contrast was striking. The finger being kept away from the sacred beads was being used to point angrily at another human being.

I began thinking about the purpose of spiritual practices.

We are so careful about the way we hold a mala, but how careful are we about the words that come out of our mouths?

We protect the beads from our index finger, but do we protect our consciousness from ego?

We pay attention to the movements of our fingers during Japa, but are we equally attentive to the movements of our own ego?

Perhaps the real purity we need to cultivate is not merely in the way we hold a mala, but in the way we hold ourselves.

As I moved towards the exit, another unexpected encounter brought my thoughts back to the meaning of service.

The entrance to the food distribution area was closed, and a few monks were standing outside, waiting to enter and receive food. Among them, I recognised someone. He was the same monk whom I had encountered earlier during my walk, when I had asked for a little help with a lift. He had ignored my request and moved away. Now, I saw him standing outside the gate, politely requesting permission to enter. I watched him and smiled quietly. It was not about the lift or any personal grievance. What stayed with me was the nature of service. If someone is walking beside us and needs a little help, isn't that an opportunity to serve? If we believe that God exists in every living being, shouldn't our first response be kindness?

I remembered my Gurudev's words:

“If you cannot recognise God in everyone, how can you claim to have found God?”

It felt as though life itself was showing me a lesson through an unexpected situation.

Perhaps wearing the identity of a sadhu is one thing, but living with the heart of a sadhu is an entirely different journey. A spiritual life should not be limited to a particular dress, a mala, a tilak, or a place of residence. It should be reflected in the way we treat others, especially when nobody is watching.

Compassion has no boundaries

As I continued reflecting on these experiences, another observation from Vrindavan came to my mind. Throughout the city, I had seen people feeding monkeys, offering fruits to cows, and giving food to birds. It was beautiful to witness. People were buying fruits and distributing them among the animals. Perhaps they were doing it out of genuine love, devotion, or the belief that such acts would bring punya, or spiritual merit.

But I began thinking about what happens after the pilgrimage.

When we return to our homes, do we continue the same practices?

Do we feed the cows near their homes?

Do we care for the birds in their neighbourhoods?

Do we show the same compassion towards animals when they are no longer surrounded by the atmosphere of Vrindavan?

Why should a cow in Vrindavan be considered sacred, while a cow elsewhere becomes just another animal?

Why should a bird need to be in a holy place to receive our kindness?

If we believe that every living being carries the presence of God, shouldn't our compassion extend everywhere?

I understand that we all have different intentions, and many perform these acts with genuine devotion. I do not wish to judge anyone. But I felt that sometimes we become so attached to the idea of performing good deeds in a sacred place that we forget to make compassion a part of our everyday lives.

It is almost as though we believe that something becomes spiritually valuable only when performed in a particular location. I wondered whether we were following the feeling of devotion or simply following what everyone around us was doing. Because genuine compassion should not depend on geography. A cow does not become sacred only when it enters Vrindavan. A bird does not become worthy of kindness only when it flies over a temple.

If our love is genuine, it should not need a sacred address.

God is everywhere: Have we forgotten to see?

All these experiences brought me to a deeper reflection on the rituals we perform in the name of devotion.

We offer flowers, light lamps, burn incense, and decorate deities. These traditions can be beautiful expressions of love and reverence. But I began looking at them from another perspective.

When our father is alive, we don't simply stand before him with flowers and incense. We serve him, offer him food, care for him, and express our love through our actions.

Perhaps this is where we need to look more deeply at our relationship with God. Do we sometimes limit our devotion to external offerings while overlooking the divine presence in everyday life?

Perhaps God is already alive in everything around us—in the soil beneath our feet, the air we breathe, the birds, the animals, and every human being. Maybe it is not God who needs awakening, but our own consciousness.

We worship love, yet struggle to love. We worship compassion, yet sometimes fail to show kindness. We offer flowers to the divine, yet may find it difficult to offer a gentle word to another human being.

Perhaps the true purpose of rituals is not merely to perform them, but to allow them to transform the way we think, feel, and live.

The true expression of Bhakti is not simply how beautifully we worship the divine, but how genuinely we embody love, humility, and compassion towards every living being.

I arrived in Vrindavan seeking an experience of God. I left with a deeper understanding that the divine is not confined to a temple or a sacred place. The soil, the air, the animals, the birds, and the people all reminded me to look beyond appearances.

A question to myself and the readers

If God is already alive in everything around us, is it really God who needs awakening by doing rituals, or is it our own consciousness?

I remembered something my Gurudev used to say:

“If you cannot see God in all, you cannot see God at all.”

Those words began echoing within me.

title: Phantom synagogues and tall tribe tales: Myths of Sri Lanka’s Jewish past | Daily FT
summary:
